JAX DNest engine: validated against the original CDNest and 16.8× faster than dynesty once a likelihood call costs ~13 ms

Date 2026-11-18 / Type full / Language en / Generated by GLM (glm-5.3-prime) via DeepSeek Harness, not human-reviewed

Bottom line

The new jnesty/dfnest module is a working JAX/GPU port of CDNest's diffusive nested sampling: it reproduces the original C code's evidence pipeline to machine precision, matches it statistically over 64 paired runs, recovers analytic evidences on all four jnesty demo problems, and is used exactly like the package's other samplers.

  • Correctness (high confidence): the C postprocessor port agrees with the original CDNest to 9.3×10−15 in logZ on identical inputs; 64-run ensembles give a 99% interval for the JAX−CDNest logZ difference of [−0.028, +0.023], inside the CDNest run-to-run spread of ±0.056.
  • Fitting (high confidence): demo evidences land within 0.037 of analytic truth (5-D mixture, 20-D Gaussian, 2-D shells), with posterior shapes recovered (radial mean 1.994 vs 2.0 on the shells).
  • Speed (medium confidence): dynesty is 18× faster on cheap likelihoods; DNest is 16.8× faster (27.4 s vs 461 s) when one likelihood call costs ~13 ms, because it batches evaluations on the GPU.
Next step: run it on a real fitting problem where the likelihood is expensive — the constructor and data format match NestedSampler and NautilusSampler one-for-one.

How the module was developed

The task was to bring CDNest (Yan-Rong Li's C/MPI implementation of Brewer's diffusive nested sampling, pinned at commit 3aaa039) into jnesty as a third engine next to the Dynesty-style and Nautilus engines, with the same loglikelihood/prior_transform data format and CDNest's per-parameter proposal-frequency feature. Diffusive nested sampling carves the likelihood into levels, learns each level's prior volume from how often particles visiting it also clear the next threshold, and lets the particle ensemble diffuse across levels — there is no live-point shrinkage as in dynesty.

The build order was chosen so every mathematical piece was pinned to the C source before the next piece was written on top of it:

  • Postprocessor first: a float64 port of CDNest's src/dnestpostprocess.c (the authority for evidence, weights and effective sample size), checked against a hand-computed three-level fixture before anything else existed.
  • Kernels second: the Metropolis particle update, the heavy-tailed level move, and the visit/exceed bookkeeping were written as pure JAX functions and fuzz-tested against literal transcriptions of the C loops (400 random cases per rule).
  • Engine third: one compiled JAX program advances num_lanes independent workers (the analogue of CDNest's MPI ranks, vmap over lanes, lax.scan over each lane's sequential steps); the host keeps everything that changes shape — level creation, volume recomputation, saves, and CDNest's root-worker lagging-particle replacement.
  • Integration last: the public DNestSampler adapter, the results bridge, FITS I/O, four demos, documentation, and 127 new tests.

Two scope decisions were confirmed with you before implementation: parity with CDNest is statistical (identical RNG trajectories are impossible across JAX and GSL and would forbid useful GPU batching), and sample_frequency is a vector of relative weights that selects which coordinate each proposal perturbs — never a modifier of acceptance ratios or posterior weights.

Findings

All four demo fits recover their analytic evidence within 0.04

Running the four existing jnesty benchmark problems through the new engine (default CDNest options, 2,000–3,000 saved particles) reproduces every analytic reference. The 20-D Gaussian also fixes an error in the older demo: the information H is computed with the correct truncated-prior formula, and the measured value lands 0.01 nats from it.

The port matches the original CDNest to machine precision and statistically

Two independent checks against the pinned C code (built in a throwaway conda environment with an archived seed-only patch; nothing from it touches jnesty at runtime). First, feeding CDNest's own raw output through the JAX postprocessor reproduces the C evidence to 9.3×10−15 across all 64 reference runs. Second, 64 paired ensembles on the 2-D Gaussian give a 99% Welch interval for the logZ difference of [−0.028, +0.023], inside CDNest's own run-to-run spread — the two engines are statistically indistinguishable, and both bracket the analytic truth.

dynesty wins by 18× on cheap likelihoods; DNest wins by 16.8× at ~13 ms per call

The honest trade-off: diffusive nested sampling evaluates far more likelihoods than dynesty's live-point scheme (2.56 M vs 35 k calls on the same 2-D problem), so with a trivial likelihood dynesty's CPU loop is simply faster. But DNest's wall time is flat at ~27.5 s across a 15,000-fold range of per-call compute cost, because the GPU absorbs the arithmetic — while dynesty's wall time grows linearly. The measured trends cross between 0.1 and 13 ms per call, and at the top tier the GPU engine is 16.8× ahead.

Using the sampler: the same callables as the other engines

DNest takes the identical (loglikelihood, prior_transform, ndim) data format, so switching engines means changing one constructor. The run control is CDNest's: max_num_saves sets how many posterior particles are saved (run length, not a convergence criterion), and ptol stops level creation. There is no per-run logzerr — the uncertainty proxy is the effective sample size n_eff, and evidence scatter comes from repeated runs, as CDNest itself recommends.

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jnesty import DNestSampler, plotting

def loglikelihood(x):                 # physical space, one scalar per point
    return -0.5 * jnp.sum(x ** 2)

def prior_transform(u):               # unit cube [0,1) -> physical space
    return (u - 0.5) * 10.0

sampler = DNestSampler(
    loglikelihood, prior_transform, ndim=5,
    num_lanes=8,                       # workers = CDNest's MPI ranks
    num_particles=2,                   # CDNest's NumberParticles, per lane
    sample_frequency=1.0,              # per-parameter proposal weights
    seed=0)

log_z = sampler.run(max_num_saves=10000)
points, log_w, log_l = sampler.posterior()   # (N, ndim), normalised weights

print(f"logZ = {log_z:.3f}  ESS = {sampler.n_eff:.0f}  "
      f"levels = {sampler.n_levels}")
res = sampler.results                  # Dynesty-style view (cached)
plotting.cornerplot(res)

The headline feature — per-parameter proposal frequencies — needs one argument. Give slowly varying parameters a smaller weight so the sampler stops spending proposals on them; the frequencies only allocate proposals, so the posterior and evidence are unchanged (verified: a [1, 3] weighting on the 2-D Gaussian reproduces the evidence within the same tolerance as uniform):

# Propose parameter 0 three times as often as parameter 1;
# never touch parameter 2 with the built-in proposal.
sampler = DNestSampler(loglikelihood, prior_transform, ndim=3,
                       sample_frequency=[3.0, 1.0, 0.0])
sampler.run(max_num_saves=5000)
print(sampler.coordinate_attempts)    # realised proposal counts per parameter

Limits and what this report does not establish

  • Benchmark confound (medium): DNest ran on GPU (CUDA), dynesty on CPU. The comparison measures each engine in its natural configuration on one machine, not an architecture-isolated one — the 16.8× figure would shrink against a compiled or parallel dynesty variant.
  • Crossover interpolated (medium): the 0.1–13 ms crossover region is bracketed by measurements, not measured point-by-point; the top-tier dynesty arm completed 4 of 5 runs before being stopped (medians over 4).
  • DNest runs are seeded-deterministic: the benchmark's five DNest runs per tier are identical by construction (same seed), so its "spread" is zero; its true run-to-run scatter (±0.054) comes from the separate 64-seed parity study.
  • Out of scope, deliberately (rejected at construction with an explicit error): level-dependent proposal limits (limits_on), plateau likelihoods, disk checkpoint/resume, and likelihood blobs. CDNest's native Gaussian/log prior kernels are not ported — jnesty prior transforms cover non-uniform priors instead, verified on an Exponential-prior test.
  • Work is uncommitted: the branch dev_cdnest holds the changes; nothing is pushed. Rollback is therefore trivially available (delete the branch), and the pre-existing suites pass unchanged, so no shipped behaviour depends on this change.

Environment: jnesty branch dev_cdnest (base 7ae194e), JAX 0.9.2 on CUDA, dynesty 2.1.4, NumPy 1.26/2.x, 48-core host.
